endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Device Software Functions: Lifecycle Management and Marketing Submission Recommendations (draft guidance)
endorsements.quote: Explanation of what the model output means and how it is intended to be used.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Determine whether decision thresholds for the AI model have been established and whether they are clear and understandable to end users when they engage with the model output.

endorsements.title: AI-driven high-risk pregnancy prediction: balancing early detection, anxiety, and discrimination in digital public health
endorsements.quote: Explainability should be communication-ready: display uncertainty, justify thresholds, and specify human–AI teaming rules so outputs are treated as decision support, not destiny ( 45 ).

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether explaining outputs, risk categories, and thresholds in labeling and interfaces reduces clinician misinterpretation, and no supplied study documents the misinterpretation hazard itself. The recommendation rests on one FDA draft guidance, one industry framework, and one commentary.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The three endorsements express expert agreement, but agreement among guidance documents does not show that labeling explanations change how clinicians read scores.

FDA draft guidance on AI-enabled device software functions asks developers to explain what model output means and how it is intended to be used. Because the guidance is in draft, it signals the agency's current thinking rather than a binding requirement. The CHAI guide adds a voluntary check on whether thresholds are clear to end users.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare clinician interpretation of AI scores, categories, and thresholds with and without structured explanations in labeling or interfaces, measuring interpretation accuracy, decision changes, and patient outcomes. Baseline studies that measure how often clinicians misread AI thresholds would also establish the size of the hazard.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Whether interface explanations work for clinicians in under-resourced settings, or whether patient-facing versions are understandable to people with limited literacy or English proficiency, remains unknown.
